power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Framing, Analysis, Interpretation and Two Supplemental Tests for Exploring Serial Mediation Theories with Cross-Sectional Data

author.affiliation:
Human Development and Family Studies
								Iowa State University

text.text: Nonexperimental cross-sectional data are frequently used to evaluate mediation and serial mediation hypotheses despite well-established limitations for such tests.
Associational Variable Analysis (AVA) was introduced to address this problem by reframing mediational language in terms of conditional associations and incremental variance.

This paper extends the framing, analysis options, and interpretation guidance in AVA to help researchers improve the analysis and interpretation of studies exploring serial mediation type theories with cross-sectional data.
Two supplemental analyses are proposed to aid in the interpretation of such data.
One symmetric conditional attenuation, measuring redundancy among the proposed set of variables.

The second conditional centrality focused on the proposed mediating variables to examine if they account for a disproportionate share of the conditional dependence relative to the putative independent and dependent variables.

Two empirical illustrations are used to demonstrate the framing, set of additional analyses needed to help frame alternative interpretations, and the utility of the two analytic summaries in terms of fostering both the completeness and accuracy of interpretation of such tests and foster incremental science.

The first example draws on the data used in the initial AVA paper and the second evaluates a published serial mediation model linking family atmosphere to suicidal ideation through attachment and cognitive flexibility.
Code and details for conducting the analyses are provided in supplemental materials.

Findings illustrate how the suggested estimates help clarify redundancy, differentiation, and structural organization within multivariable theories thereby providing interpretive guidance for cross-sectional analyses where serial mediation conclusions are not defensible.

Nonexperimental cross-sectional data (NECSD) continue to be widely used to test hypotheses with mediational and serial mediational goals, despite extensive theoretical and empirical work demonstrating that such designs cannot support causal or temporal claims about intervening processes (Cole & Maxwell, 2003; Maxwell & Cole, 2007; O'Laughlin et al., 2018; Weems, 2025).
text.formatted: Nonexperimental cross-sectional data (NECSD) continue to be widely used to test hypotheses with mediational and serial mediational goals, despite extensive theoretical and empirical work demonstrating that such designs cannot support causal or temporal claims about intervening processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cole & Maxwell, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Maxwell & Cole, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">O'Laughlin et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Weems, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While the myriad problems are well-detailed in the literature, one main issue worth noting here is that framing cross-sectional analyses as mediation risks creating a misleading depiction of a particular literature, by incorrectly identifying causal or temporally intermediary processes.
Despite the reasons to not frame such studies as mediation, its likely authors will continue if viable alternatives are not available (Weems, 2025).
text.formatted: Despite the reasons to not frame such studies as mediation, its likely authors will continue if viable alternatives are not available <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Weems, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, initial crosssectional tests of mediational type theories can have value but need clear framing and complementary analytic tools.

Weems (2025) presented Associational Variable Analysis (AVA) as an alternative conceptual framework and set of steps that retain a set of common analytic tools, while explicitly constraining inference to patterns of association and overlap that are identifiable from contemporaneous data.
By reframing mediational language in terms of incremental validity and conditional associations, AVA provides a way to frame, analyze and reduce inferential overreach.

The present paper extends Weems (2025) by defining and exploring ways to estimate a potential associational variable's influence that may help capture distinct properties of multivariable dependence in cases where there are more than three variables of interest.

The Weems (2025) paper used the term associational variable for mediator and indirect association to denote a non-causal version of the indirect effect but left how to deal with theories involving Conditional Associations 4 chain or serial mediation largely unaddressed.
The issues are ones of both terminology and analysis.

Serial or chain mediation is said to occur when the effect of an independent variable on a dependent variable is conveyed through multiple mediators (causal intermediary processes) that operate in a hypothesized causal and or temporal order.
In an NECSD study, such a process cannot be truly discovered.

A set of cross-sectional associations may be more or less consistent with the theory and thereby provide initial evidence that conducting a more difficult longitudinal or experimental study may be useful.

The goal in this paper is to further extend the reframing of mediational language in terms of conditional associations and provide an improved framework for evaluating serial mediation theories using NECSD.
A set of complementary analytic techniques to augment such studies are outlined with their logical basis and examples of framing and interpreting such data with the techniques are provided.

It is useful to start with the concept of partial correlation which is often defined as the correlation between X and Y conditional on Z. From this definition, an associational variable in AVA is a conditional variable or conditioning variable (CV) and indirect association, the conditional association (CA) 1 .
Starting with three variables, let (𝑋𝑋, 𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶, 𝑌𝑌) we can denote three observed variables measured contemporaneously, with covariance matrix Σ and correlation matrix 𝑅𝑅.
The basic question that a NECSD can address is to quantify change in zero-order association between 𝑋𝑋 and 𝑌𝑌 once the CV is conditioned on it.

A typical conditional association in a mediational theory can be defined as the directional difference between the zero-order association and the conditioned association, and so can have positive (conditional association is smaller), zero (no difference), or negative (conditional association is larger) values.

Positive values indicate attenuation of the focal association when conditioning on the CV, whereas negative values indicate amplification or suppression (i.e., cases in which the conditioned association exceeds the zero-order association in magnitude) which is standard partial correlation math in regression analysis (MacKinnon et al., 2000).

text.text: In hypotheses involving two or more variables as intermediary processes (serial mediation), a common approach is to conduct a structural equation model testing the relative fit of different configurations and/or conduct indirect effects decomposition with software such as the PROCESS macro with the intermediary variables between the theoretically primary independent variable and main outcome (Hayes, 2022; JASP Team, 2025; Kline, 2023).

text.text: If the study uses NECSD, one may simply frame this test as associational; however, only testing the single hypothesized set of associations leaves several alternative interpretations of the findings untested.
Thus, the results and their interpretation are ambiguous (MacCallum et al., 1993).

text.text: This ambiguity and failure of causal or temporal logic has been understood and noted for some time.
Because of this, authors have suggested 1) conducting a set of alternative model analyses to help rule out alternative interpretations (see e.g., Hayes, 2022; Tomarken & Waller, 2003).

text.text: For example, Kline (2023) provides detailed coverage of how to and the importance of comparing alternative models fitted with the same data as part of standard SEM practice.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kline (2023)</ref> provides detailed coverage of how to and the importance of comparing alternative models fitted with the same data as part of standard SEM practice.

text.text: In addition to alternative model fit and path coefficients 2) a simple approach is to conduct and compare the set of all possible partial correlations and examine relative patterns of change from the zero-order to the conditional association (similar to the suggestion in Weems, 2025 for a three variable structure).
Both are important to interpret the results of NECSD.

However, neither 1) alternative-model comparisons within SEM nor 2) inspection of partial-correlation patterns directly summarizes two potentially informative features of a multivariable set of associations implied by serial mediation theories.
These are (A) the overall degree of symmetric conditional attenuation across the full set of variables and (B) the relative concentration of conditional association within particular variables.

These features are currently not common targets of conventional mediation analyses, alternative-model comparisons, or pairwise partial-correlation approaches, but such estimates may provide useful information for interpreting the viability of serial mediation type theories with NECSD.
Theoretically, in terms of (A) an affirmative test of a serial mediation theory with NECSD might be characterized by moderate symmetrical overlap.
This is because some redundancy is expected if the mediators account for the predictor-outcome association.

In terms of (B) the putative mediators should exhibit conditional centrality comparable to or greater than that of the predictor or dependent variable -should not appear structurally peripheral within a conditional dependence system implied by a theoretical model.

In other words, a favorable associational pattern for a serial mediation theory in NECSD would be one in which conditional centrality is concentrated in the proposed mediating variables rather than primarily in the predictor or outcome.

Thus, a serial mediation theory receives stronger associational support: (A) when the variables exhibit a moderate degree of symmetric conditional attenuation, indicating meaningful but not overwhelming redundancy among the proposed variables, and (B) when conditional centrality is focused on the proposed mediating variables such that they account for a disproportionate share of the model's conditional dependence relative to the putative independent and dependent variables.
Such a pattern is consistent with the theoretical claim that associations between the predictor and outcome are organized around intermediary constructs.
The following sections develop the logic for calculating estimates of symmetric conditional attenuation, and conditional centrality based on existing formulations.
One way to think about patterns of associational overlap is what happens to the set of individual associations when all variables are conditioned.
While the basic logic of conducing a series of partial correlations focuses and gives primacy to a single pair (𝑋𝑋, 𝑌𝑌).
A generalized approach can be extended to a larger set testing all the various combinations to characterize the entire multivariable system of four or more variables.
One avenue is to calculate how much total pairwise association changes once all variables are mutually conditioned.

Negative SCA values therefore indicate results in which mutual conditioning increases, rather than diminishes, the magnitude of pairwise associations.

The SCA formula draws directly on established calculations with partial correlations used to characterize residual pairwise associations after accounting for shared dependence with other variables (Lauritzen, 1996; Waldorp & Marsman, 2022) as well as redundancy-focused diagnostics of multivariate association in regression (Timme et al., 2013).

text.text: The goal of this Conditional Associations 24 paper was to extend AVA by highlighting the importance of patterns of partial correlations and introducing two complementary descriptive summaries to help characterize features of associational results implied by serial mediation theories.
Within an AVA framework, SCA and CC provide estimates to aid in evaluating serial mediation-type theories with NECSD.
SCA summarizes the extent to which observed associations reflect shared versus conditionally specific dependence across the full set of variables.
CC summarizes where the remaining conditional dependence is concentrated once shared dependence has been removed.

Viewed together, SCA and CC move beyond the logic of pairwise attenuation by describing both the degree of redundancy in a set of variables and the relative structural involvement of individual variables.
These estimates can help guide interpretations by providing information that complements traditional common analyses.

Theoretically, stronger associational support would be expected when variables exhibit a moderate degree of shared dependence and when conditional dependence is concentrated in the proposed mediating variables.
The examples illustrate how SCA and CC can inform the interpretation of serial mediation-type theories in NECSD.

Thus, common-method diagnostics evaluate a possible source of covariance, whereas the proposed measures characterize how the observed association changes under mutual conditioning.
The approaches suggested here can be considered complementary with the diagnostics for common method variance as part of an analytic pipeline.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.
The illustrative examples were selected to demonstrate interpretation and should not be taken as establishing normative values for SCA or CC.
The practical meaning of low, moderate, or high redundancy will likely vary across domains as a function of construct overlap, measurement characteristics, and typical effect sizes.

Additional work is needed to examine the sampling properties of the estimates, investigate robustness to measurement error and suppression effects, and establish domain-specific benchmarks through replication.
Future work might also explore extensions to latent-variable SEM frameworks, longitudinal designs, and alternative forms of conditional dependence estimation.
The proposed interpretation framework should be regarded as descriptive rather than inferential.
Neither SCA nor CC provides evidence regarding temporal ordering, causal processes, or mediation.

Instead, the estimates summarize properties of observed correlational results and are therefore consistent with the central purpose of AVA: constraining interpretation to inferences that are supported by contemporaneously measured data (Weems, 2025).

Consistent with this perspective, the value of the suggested supplemental tests is likely to through cumulative comparisons across studies, rather than through specific thresholds.

In conclusion, this paper extends the framing, analysis options, and interpretation guidance in AVA to help researchers improve the analysis and interpretation of tests of chain mediation type theories with cross-sectional data.

Theoretically, a serial mediation theory receives stronger associational support: (A) when the variables exhibit a moderate degree of symmetric conditional attenuation and (B) when conditional centrality is focused on the proposed mediating variables relative to the putative independent and dependent variables.
SCA quantifies the degree to which association is shared across a set of variables, whereas CC identifies where conditional dependence is concentrated.

When used alongside partial correlations, regression analyses, or SEM model comparisons, examining the patterns of partial correlations and the supplemental tests proposed may help researchers more completely characterize the associational structure implied by serial mediation theories within the limitations of NECSD.

All analyses reported here represent a secondary reanalysis of these data and were conducted independently of the original authors.
According to Yang et al. they used a cross-sectional survey design in which participants completed a battery of self-report questionnaires administered in a single assessment session.
Data were collected from 856 Chinese college students recruited from universities in China.
Participants ranged in age from 18 to 28 years, and the sample included both male and female students.
All measures assessed current perceptions or experiences, and no experimental manipulation or longitudinal follow-up was involved.
Yang et al. assessed family atmosphere, attachment style, cognitive flexibility, and suicidal ideation using standardized self-report measures administered to Chinese college students.

Family atmosphere was measured with the Family Atmosphere subscale of the Self-Rating Scale of Systemic Family Dynamics, which assesses perceived emotional climate, communication, and interpersonal functioning within the family.

Attachment was assessed using the Relationship Questionnaire (RQ), which yields continuous scores for four attachment styles-secure, fearful, preoccupied, and dismissive-with Yang et al.'s primary analyses emphasizing fearful attachment.

Cognitive flexibility was measured with the Cognitive Flexibility Inventory (CFI), including both the control and alternatives subscales, with cognitive flexibility serving as the focal mediator in their main chain-mediation model.
Suicidal ideation was assessed using the Self-Rated Ideation of Suicide Scale (SRIS), with total ideation scores used in the primary analyses.

The pattern of partial correlations, the symmetric conditional share, and the conditional-centrality estimates provide information about relative importance, redundancy, and structural organization within the observed associational system.

Consistent with Yang et al.'s conclusions, fearful attachment and cognitive flexibility participate in the association between family atmosphere and suicidal ideation, and conditioning on these variables attenuates the family atmosphere-suicidal ideation association.
However, the analyses also reveal asymmetries that are not evident from their mediation model alone.
Consistent with Yang et al.'s interpretation, cognitive flexibility does appear to have a more proximal position relative to suicidal ideation than fearful attachment.
However, conditionalcentrality analysis indicated that the dominant feature of the set of variables was not one of the proposed chain of intermediary variables.

Instead, suicidal ideation accounted for the largest Conditional Associations 23 share of total conditional dependence, with fearful attachment contributing the smallest share.This pattern suggests that the observed associational structure is organized at least as much around suicidal ideation as around the hypothesized mediating processes.

Moreover, several of the largest reductions in pairwise associations occur when conditioning on suicidal ideation itself, suggesting that the observed covariance structure is organized at least as much around suicidal ideation as around the proposed intermediary variables.

Thus, while the data are consistent with Yang et al.'s hypothesized variables being involved in the observed pattern of associations, the results do not support an interpretation in which attachment and cognitive flexibility function as sequential intermediary processes.

Rather, the findings indicate a moderately redundant set of variables in which suicidal ideation, cognitive flexibility, family atmosphere, and fearful attachment are interrelated, with suicidal ideation emerging as the most structurally central variable.
